content.text: The text combines Descartes’ defense of publishing his philosophical method with extensive Civil War fiction. Descartes favors orderly inquiry, evidence, humility, and useful knowledge of nature, rejecting scholastic obscurity and empty reputation. The narrative follows Kentucky youth Fred Shackelford, who chooses the Union despite his Confederate father and cousin Calhoun. Fred travels through Kentucky, joins General Nelson at Camp Dick Robinson, scouts Georgetown, Lexington, Elizabethtown, and Cumberland, and serves Thomas, Sherman, and Grant. He repeatedly gathers intelligence, disrupts Confederate operations, survives capture, and fights at Mill Springs, Fort Donelson, and Shiloh. He reunites with his wounded father and later reconciles with him. Parallel social fiction follows Ruth’s departure and reconciliation with Easton, Owen’s poverty and labor activism in Mugsborough, Hunter’s suicide, Barrington’s socialist commitments, and his Christmas aid to poor children.
